nicheStories.title: Pakistan thought it won the peace. Now, it could be dragged into war.
nicheStories.description: Four weeks ago, Pakistan looked like one of the biggest winners of the U.S.-Iran war.Its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, shuttled between Washington, Tehran and Gulf capitals for months. As part of his efforts, Pakistan hosted the first face-to-face U.S.-Iran talks in years and helped broker the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that Vice President JD Vance signed in June, thanking Munir and calling him one of the “very, very important people” in his life.Islamabad hired a Washington lobbying firm to convert that goodwill into defense cooperation and minerals investment, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif spoke of a “sun of progress and prosperity” for Pakistan’s chronically stressed economy after the MoU between the U.S.and Iran brought an end to major military operations.Pakistan's fortunes have since reversed. Fighting between Washington and Tehran has resumed, and Islamabad’s dual goals of being Iran’s trusted interlocutor and the Arab Gulf states’ security guarantor are once again at odds.President Donald Trump declared the deal was “over” in early July, after which the U.S. struck civilian and military targets in Iran. Iran, for its part, declared on July 18 through its deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, that it was “suspending all obligations” under the framework. The war has since widened into exactly the kind of multi-front regional conflict Pakistan spent the spring trying to prevent.The clearest new exposure for Pakistan is in Saudi Arabia, where Iran struck Prince Sultan Air Base at al-Kharj — its first direct hit on Saudi territory since March — just days after the Houthis, Iran’s Yemeni ally, fired missiles on the kingdom, hitting Abha airport in the country’s south. That escalation occurred after Saudi-allied forces hit Sanaa airport in Yemen to prevent the landing of an Iranian airliner; the U.S. Treasury alleged without providing evidence that the plane is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp. The strikes effectively enforced Riyadh’s airspace veto over the Houthi-controlled capital.Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact with Riyadh last year. It deployed fighter jets and thousands of troops to the kingdom after earlier Iranian strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure. More recently, Islamabad has reportedly communicated to Tehran directly that attacks on Saudi Arabia will be treated as attacks on Pakistan itself. Sharif’s own statement in the aftermath called the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia a violation of the kingdom’s sovereignty that Pakistan “strongly condemns,” pledging “unwavering support” for Riyadh's security.The tone is notable given that Pakistan’s parliament explicitly refused to get entangled in Yemen over a decade ago. In April 2015, faced with a nearly identical Saudi request to join the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, Pakistan’s National Assembly voted unanimously to “maintain neutrality.” Islamabad’s calculus has not changed. If anything, recent events have sharpened Pakistan’s desire to broker a lasting peace.Pakistan is home to the world’s second-largest Shia population after Iran, and the killing of Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, in February set off deadly unrest in Karachi and Islamabad; Munir himself had to intervene to calm a wave of processions and pledges of allegiance to the new supreme leader across Shia neighborhoods.Significantly, Munir and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif attended Khamenei’s funeral in July, and Sharif posted after that "the late Supreme Leader’s wisdom, leadership and profound influence on Iran and the wider region will be remembered for generations" — a demonstration of the fine line Pakistan’s leadership has to walk, one no doubt delivered with a domestic audience in mind as much as an Iranian one.That fine line becomes impossible to walk when a defense pact, triggered by Saudi-Houthi fighting or by further Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia, would ask Pakistan to do the exact thing its parliament explicitly refused a decade ago: take a military side against a Houthi-Iran axis, and do so at a moment when its domestic Shia politics is highly combustible.Kuwait is now reportedly asking for the same kind of commitment that Saudi Arabia already has. Reuters reported last week that Islamabad is in early-stage talks with Kuwait — which has absorbed repeated Iranian strikes on its infrastructure in recent days — over an expanded defense agreement that would include "thousands of Pakistani troops on the ground, fighter jets, drones, an air defence system, and other defence-related facilities," according to an anonymous Pakistani government official cited in the report.Another anonymous Pakistani security official said the country “cannot consider a deployment of combat troops at this stage." That hesitation suggests that stacking multiple defense commitments across Gulf states in Iran’s crosshairs makes Islamabad’s balancing act much harder to sustain. Each new pact narrows the room to claim neutrality the next time Tehran calls.During this war, Pakistan discovered what happens when Gulf partners doubt its ability to balance between Tehran and the Arab Gulf states. The United Arab Emirates recalled a $3.5 billion loan in April and quietly began deporting Pakistani Shia workers by the thousands. The move was widely read as retaliation for Islamabad's perceived tilt toward Tehran during the mediation. Saudi Arabia stepped in with $3 billion to cover the gap, but the lesson was clear: Pakistan’s neutrality satisfies no one fully, and the cost of disappointing any single Gulf patron is measured in the billions of dollars.Economic self-preservation has been Pakistan’s primary motive for steering mediation and ending a war that has hobbled the economies of its creditors and choked the trade routes that power its own electric grid. Pakistan is on its 25th International Monetary Fund program; more than half of its tax revenue is put towards servicing its debts. It had barely stabilized its inflation before the Strait of Hormuz's closure sent rates back into double digits.In March, as the war’s first phase disrupted energy flows out of Hormuz, Islamabad ordered a two-week school closure and imposed a four-day work week to conserve fuel — measures the government has now indicated it may need to revive.A parallel disruption to the Red Sea, like the blockade of Saudi Arabia declared by the Houthis Monday, would be highly disruptive to Pakistan’s energy security, and by extension, its economy. While Pakistan imports the overwhelming majority of its fuel from the Gulf, the closing of another critical chokepoint would simultaneously tighten global tanker capacity and insurance costs everywhere, pushing the same spot-market prices Pakistan is already struggling to afford even higher.It would also add further pressure on Pakistan’s defense commitments to Saudi Arabia, given that Riyadh will not tolerate such a closure. In a recent statement, Riyadh pledged to deal with “Houthi threats against transiting vessels…firmly and swiftly.” The stakes for Saudi Arabia are high: Since the Strait of Hormuz was blocked, Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West pipeline to divert roughly 5 million barrels per day of crude to the Red Sea Port of Yanbu — its only viable export outlet while Hormuz is all but closed.None of this means Pakistan’s mediation was a mistake, or that its diplomatic capital has evaporated. Kuwait’s foreign minister still thanked Pakistan last week for its “constructive and mediatory role,” and Islamabad remains one of the few channels through which Washington and Tehran would resume talks, when the time comes. But the specific bet Pakistan made — that ending the war would allow it to bank the goodwill through commerce and financial aid — has not yet paid off.Instead, the restart of the war has brought Saudi Arabia back into Iran’s crosshairs. At the same time, the Saudi-Houthi front has reopened, the Strait of Hormuz has been closed again, and a blockade of Saudi-linked ships on the Red Sea has been formally declared.Each of these factors adds immense pressure on Pakistan, which now has every reason to double down on diplomacy, lest it be drawn in as a combatant.

nicheStories.title: The Zumwalt-class destroyer is an ever-growing boondoggle
nicheStories.description: After ten years of upgrades, repairs, and program-related issues, the lead Zumwalt-class destroyer is finally returning to service this September. But it will have to go without the hypersonic missiles many hoped would give the troubled program a purpose.Thanks to ongoing modernization efforts, the lead Zumwalt-class destroyer now has a launcher, making it the Navy’s first hypersonic strike ship. But the missiles themselves will not be tested until next year, as the Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) hypersonic missile rollout is about two years behind schedule.Experts tell RS the problem is par for the course for the Zumwalt program.“The Zumwalt program had extraordinary promise,” Ben Freeman, the director of the Quincy Institute’s Democratizing Foreign Policy program, wrote to RS. “But it was curtailed from 32 ships to just 3 for a reason: it didn't come close to living up to that promise.”The Zumwalt’s initial role as a land-attack ship was scrapped in 2016 after ammunition for its land-attack gun became prohibitively costly, reaching $800,000 to $1 million per round. Beyond that, “they couldn't get the [ship’s] weapon to work properly,” Dan Grazier, who directs the Stimson Center’s National Security Reform program, told RS. In the end, the military built three Zumwalts at a cost of $9.5 billion per ship. Now, efforts to convert the remaining into hypersonic strike ships have only steered the program into more procurement issues.“They foisted an unproven missile system with its own checkered acquisition history onto the Zumwalt seemingly in hopes that two wrongs would make a right,” Freeman said. “Spoiler: they didn't.”The Pentagon plans to invest $50 billion into developing and fielding its CPS hypersonic capability across Army and Navy programs. But a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published last week found the project "does not have a comprehensive strategy" to accomplish its objectives.Canceled and failed test flights and quality control issues also plague the hypersonic missile program. One test, for example, was canceled in 2023 after a battery failure during a pre-launch check. Lockheed Martin can only make six or seven hypersonic missiles each year, short of the military’s target of 12 missiles, jeopardizing the program’s ability to scale. Meanwhile, costs are compounding for the Zumwalt, with questionable payoff. The hypersonic missile capability will tack on about $452 million to the cost of each destroyer. Each ship will only be able to carry 12 hypersonic missiles, which leaves them with far fewer munitions than their naval counterparts. The missiles themselves are estimated to cost tens of millions of dollars each.As Freeman concluded, “taxpayer dollars will still be wasted until the Navy comes to its senses.”

nicheStories.title: Israel targets X users, right-wing media with $2 million ad push
nicheStories.description: The Israeli government paid a Republican Party-aligned public affairs company $9.9 million to advertise and promote content in American social media and news sites, according to a new disclosure made to the Department of Justice. The firm, Targeted Communications Global, purchased nearly $2 million in ads on the social media platform X, $40,000 in conservative media outlet Breitbart, and $7,500 in the Daily Caller.Targeted Communications’ work for Israel appears to be among the most lucrative active foreign lobbying contracts in the U.S. Driving it are prominent Republican strategists seeking to book pro-Israel voices on TV programs while overseeing ad campaigns seen by hundreds of millions of people. As part of its work for Israel, Targeted Communications oversaw a now-dormant ad campaign called “Freedom Not Terror.” Starting in October 2025, the campaign began posting clips on TikTok, Instagram, X, YouTube, and Facebook. It appears to have found the most success on YouTube, garnering more than 224 million views across all of its videos. One of the videos, titled “Religious Freedom,” claims that Iran “built sleeper cells in the U.S.” The ad, which has over 23 million views, features an interview with former Israeli Ambassador to the U.S. Michael Oren, who says that “young people have been educated to believe that the most sacred thing they can do is stab a Christian in the heart.” The Freedom Not Terror accounts have not been active since December of last year. Freedom Not Terror’s most viewed post on X, a 90-second video with 1.7 million views, positions Israel as a peace-seeking nation. “America, Israel, and Arab nations agreed on a plan to bring peace to the Middle East. Hamas and radicalized Palestinians want to continue their culture of hate and reign of terror,” says the narrator. (At the time the video was posted, human rights group Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor said the Israeli army was engaged in routine violations of the ceasefire, including daily bombardment, gunfire, and destruction of homes in Gaza.)Targeted Communications’ deal with the Israeli government is being subcontracted through Havas Media, a French public relations conglomerate. Havas has hired seven subcontractors in the U.S. that have registered to work for Israel under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) in the past year. Most recently, Havas hired Daniel Rosenberg, the producer of Spike Lee’s “Inside Man,” on a $900,000 contract to produce pro-Israel media content.A spokesperson for the conservative news site The Daily Caller said their publication was not aware they were doing business with the Israeli government when they sold advertising space to representatives of Targeted Communications last October.“We had no direct transaction with either the Government of Israel or Havas Media Group. The ad buyer was listed as LAPAM and our rep was unaware of what that entity was,” The Daily Caller communications manager Conor Coutts told Responsible Statecraft. LAPAM is the Hebrew acronym for the Israeli Government Advertising Agency, which produces the ads featured in The Daily Caller, X, Breitbart, and YouTube. The Daily Caller has published a number of articles in recent weeks that are critical of Israel’s new influence campaigns. Throughout the fall of 2025, Targeted Communications also pitched news content or guests to CNN, Fox News, Newsnation, BBC, the California Post, and other mainstream news outlets, according to communications documented in the filing. The firm facilitated “TV bookings,” “media pitches,” and “PR management” with these news outlets, contacting Fox News the most (48 times), followed by CNN (22), NewsNation (13), and Newsmax (10). Targeted Communications’ ad payments in conservative media mirror some of the work of former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale, who is overseeing a $46.5 million contract with the Israeli government. Parscale has funneled $500,000 worth of ads into Salem Media Representatives, a subsidiary of Salem Media, a right-wing media conglomerate. Parscale is also running a mass texting campaign, creating websites to manipulate AI chatbot results, and integrating pro-Israel messaging into conservative media, as Responsible Statecraft previously revealed. A majority of the foreign agents on the Targeted Communications contract are listed as staff of an affiliate organized, Targeted Victory, a go-to consultancy for Republican candidates. Its current and past clients include Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Tim Scott (R-S.C.), and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) as well as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Both Targeted Communications and Targeted Victory are subsidiaries of Stagwell Group.Neither Targeted Communications nor Targeted Victory responded to requests for comment.  A few of the registered foreign agents involved in the Targeted Communications contract are also media figures. Matthew Gorman, Chief Communications Officer at Targeted Victory, is an NBC contributor at the same time as he is working for Israel. NBC’s Meet the Press does not disclose Gorman’s work moonlighting for the Israeli government. Targeted Communications communicated with NBC about TV bookings on at least three occasions.David Sable, vice-chairman of Stagwell, wrote publicly about Israel while working on the contract. Sable penned two pieces in a blog published by the Times of Israel, which did not disclose to readers that he is a registered foreign agent of Israel. The Israeli government also made two separate payments of $500,000 and $250,000 to an unnamed “U.S.-based consulting firm” in 2025. Under FARA, any contractor or subcontractor representing a foreign government is typically identified by name to the DOJ and the public. This is because FARA requires “a degree of specificity necessary to permit meaningful public evaluation” of the actions of lobbyists on behalf of foreign government clients. So long as Targeted Communications withholds the name of this consulting firm, Americans have no way of knowing which companies are operating on behalf of Israel.Ben Freeman, the director of the Quincy Institute’s Democratizing Foreign Policy program, said that if a company is directing $750,000 to an unknown firm on behalf of a foreign government, it has to disclose who that consulting firm is.“FARA is a transparency statute, and that’s the most basic level of transparency. It’s also very odd that all the other receipts of Israeli money are disclosed except this one,” said Freeman. “It really makes you wonder what they’re trying to hide here.”Stagwell, the parent company of Targeted Communications, has engaged in plenty of other pro-Israel work. Last year, Israel hired another subsidiary of Stagwell — a Democratic-aligned firm known as SKDK — on a $600,000 deal. The scope of SKDK’s work included running a “bot-based program” to amplify pro–Israel narratives on Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, YouTube, and other platforms. A day after the investigative outlet Sludge revealed that part of the firm’s work involved a bot program, SKDK revealed that it was cutting its contract with the Israeli government. A spokesperson from the firm told Politico that its work was “focused solely on media relations and nothing else.” Ultimately, Israel paid SKDK a total of $150,000 for its work. SKDK also runs the 10/7 Project, a public relations initiative to promote bipartisan support for Israel. A Gallup poll earlier this year showed that more Americans sympathize with Palestinians (41%) than Israelis (36%). Mark Penn — CEO of Stagwell, the parent company of Targeted Communications and SKDK — blamed misinformation for the cratering of public support for Israel in a December interview with the Jerusalem Post. “[Young people] don’t know which side is democratic. They don’t know about gay rights in Israel. They don’t know the basics,” said Penn. Penn is still optimistic about delivering for his Israeli government clients, pointing in particular to young people who don’t have set views on the issue. “You can win back a lot of that 15% that’s confused or misinformed,” he said.
